explanations.explanation: A cave it is. David takes refuge in the cave of Adullam after he leaves Gath. A cave is a solid hiding spot, though I bet the echo makes every whisper sound like an announcement. This is where David's story picks up.

The forest does show up in this passage, just a little later. David goes to the forest of Hereth after the prophet Gad speaks to him (1 Samuel 22:5). Adullam is where he takes refuge first, and the text calls it a cave. Hold on to that forest, because it's coming.
The text doesn't put David in a valley. It says he takes refuge in the cave of Adullam. A wide-open valley would be like hiding behind a window. A cave gives a man somewhere to actually disappear.

His brothers and the rest of his father's household hear about it, and they go down to him there. The text doesn't say why they came, so I won't tell you. I think it had to mean something that family showed up at a cave. Nobody sends a fruit basket to a cave, so showing up in person says a lot.

Nothing in the text says they report David to anybody. The verse says they heard about it and went down to him there. David's family walks toward him, not toward Saul. Saul, by the way, is the king of Israel who is after David.
That's the opposite of what happens. The text says they went down to David at the cave. They didn't stay home and wait for news. They made the trip.

Leader is right. Everyone who was distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around David, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him. That's a whole crowd gathering around a man who was hiding in a cave.
The text doesn't call David their servant. It says he became their leader. Four hundred men rallied around him, and nobody was handing him a towel. They gathered to him.

A guest gets welcomed into somebody else's place. These men rallied around David, and the verse says he became their leader. That's a different job from guest. It's closer to being the one who has to figure out where four hundred people are going to sleep.

David says, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me.” He's talking to the king of Moab at Mizpeh of Moab. David asks for a safe place for his parents, and he says out loud that he's waiting to learn what God will do for him. I like that he put it in those words.

Saul is the one chasing David, but he isn't the one in David's sentence. David says he's waiting to learn what God will do for him (1 Samuel 22:3). The waiting is on God, not on the man with the spear.

Achish is the king of Gath, the place David just left (1 Samuel 21:10-15). David is talking to the king of Moab here. And the sentence says he's waiting to learn what God will do for him. That name belongs right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: Leave the stronghold and go into Judah
explanations.explanation: Gad, a prophet, tells David, “Do not stay in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” David listens and goes to the forest of Hereth. When a prophet says move, David moves. No arguing, no packing for three more days.

explanations.answer: Stay in the stronghold and wait there
explanations.explanation: Gad says the opposite. His words are, “Do not stay in the stronghold.” The word for David is to go, and the place he's told to go is the land of Judah. David packs up and leaves.

explanations.answer: Go back to Achish in the city of Gath
explanations.explanation: Gad never sends David back to Gath. He says to go into the land of Judah. Going back to Achish, the king of Gath, would also mean returning to the place where David had to act insane to get out (1 Samuel 21:10-15). That would be a hard thing to explain at the door.

Saul asks, “Is that why all of you have conspired against me?” He's speaking to his servants, the men of Benjamin, with his spear in hand. He asks whether David is giving them fields and vineyards and making them commanders. Conspiring is the charge, and it comes out of Saul's own mouth.

Saul doesn't say anything about desertion. His words are, “Is that why all of you have conspired against me?” The charge is about a conspiracy, and Saul says it to the whole group. Nobody in the verse is accused of walking off the field.

Nobody is accused of stealing in Saul's speech. He asks if David is handing out fields and vineyards, then says, “Is that why all of you have conspired against me?” The charge is conspiracy. Saul's storehouse never comes up.

explanations.answer: David come to Ahimelech at Nob
explanations.explanation: Doeg the Edomite says, “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob.” Ahimelech is the priest at Nob. Doeg stands among Saul's servants and says what he saw. I think the room got very quiet right after that.
Doeg never mentions Samuel, the prophet who anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13), and he never mentions Ramah. What he says is that he saw David come to Ahimelech at Nob. Nob is the place in his report.

explanations.answer: David meet Jonathan in the field
explanations.explanation: Doeg says nothing about Jonathan, Saul's son (1 Samuel 14:1), or any field. His report is that he saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob. Saul was already upset about his son's covenant with David, but that's not the part Doeg speaks up about.

Doeg says the opposite. He says Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for David and gave him provisions. He also says Ahimelech gave David the sword of Goliath the Philistine. Goliath was the giant David defeated (1 Samuel 17:50). Doeg's report is that David left with a lot.

False is right. Doeg tells Saul that Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for David and gave him provisions. He also says Ahimelech gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine, the giant David defeated (1 Samuel 17:50). David didn't leave with nothing. Doeg's report listed what he got.

explanations.answer: So David could rise up against him
explanations.explanation: Saul says Ahimelech did it all “…so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.” Bread, a sword and inquiring of God are the three things on his list. That's Saul's accusation in Saul's words. Ahimelech has an answer for it, and it's coming next.

explanations.answer: So David could make peace with him
explanations.explanation: Peace isn't what Saul says. He says it was “…so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.” Saul believes David is lying in wait against him. Peace isn't anywhere in his charge.

explanations.answer: So David could fight the Philistines
explanations.explanation: The Philistines never come up in Saul's accusation. He says the bread, the sword and the inquiring were “…so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.” It's about David rising up against Saul. Saul is the one pointing the finger.

Ahimelech says it right to Saul's face: “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house?” Saul is the king, and this is a priest talking to him. That's some nerve with a king sitting there holding a spear. Ahimelech says it anyway.

It's true, because Ahimelech does say it. His words are, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house?” He says this to King Saul himself. He speaks up for David in front of the king.

Ahimelech says, “…your servant knew nothing of this whole affair—not in part or in whole.” He asks the king not to accuse him or anyone in his father's household. He's pleading, and he says his whole house knew nothing. It's the plainest way to say it.

Everything is the opposite of what Ahimelech says. His words are, “…your servant knew nothing of this whole affair—not in part or in whole.” He's pleading with Saul not to accuse him or his father's household. Saying he knew everything wouldn't help his plea.
Plenty isn't in his plea. Ahimelech says, “…your servant knew nothing of this whole affair—not in part or in whole.” He says it twice over, in part or in whole. Nothing means nothing.

Saul doesn't spare him. The king replies, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!” This is a heavy moment, and it's okay to say so. Ahimelech spoke up and the answer was still no.

False is right, and it's a heavy one. Saul answers Ahimelech, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!” He doesn't spare anyone after hearing the plea. I think this is a hard verse to sit with.

They don't obey. The text says, “But the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.” Saul gave the order, and his men wouldn't do it. I think that took courage, standing there in front of the king.

False is right. Saul orders the guards at his side to kill the priests of the LORD, but “the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.” They refuse. The order then goes to someone else.

Abiathar, one of the sons of Ahimelech, escapes and flees to David. He's the one who gets away from Nob. Then Abiathar tells David that Saul has killed the priests of the LORD. He's carrying very hard news.

Saul is the one who gave the order, so he's the last place Abiathar would run. The text says Abiathar, one of Ahimelech's sons, escaped and fled to David. Abiathar goes toward the man Saul is hunting.
Achish is the king of Gath, where David was earlier (1 Samuel 21:10-15). The text doesn't send Abiathar there. It says he escaped and fled to David.

explanations.answer: Doeg was there and was sure to tell Saul
explanations.explanation: David says, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul.” Doeg is the man who spoke up in front of Saul. David says it to Abiathar, the priest's son who just brought him the news. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Saul's guards were watching the road
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention guards or a road. He says, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul.” The name David gives is Doeg. That's all he says about that day.

explanations.answer: Achish was waiting for him in Gath
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say anything about Achish, the king of Gath, to Abiathar. His words are, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul.” The one he names is Doeg. Gath isn't in this part of the conversation.

David says, “I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house.” He says it to Abiathar, the son who escaped. David doesn't pass the blame to anybody. He takes it on himself, and he says it plainly.

Blameless isn't the word David uses. He says, “I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house.” That's him owning it. I think that's a hard thing to say to someone who just lost his family.

The text doesn't have David say he's praying. His words are, “I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house.” The word he uses is responsible. He's talking about Abiathar's whole family.

explanations.answer: Stay with him and not be afraid
explanations.explanation: David tells Abiathar, “Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.” The one after Abiathar is the same one after David. So David puts them side by side. For a man who just lost his family, I bet that offer meant a lot.

explanations.answer: Hide in Moab with David's parents
explanations.explanation: David did leave his parents with the king of Moab (1 Samuel 22:3-4), but he doesn't send Abiathar there. He says, “Stay with me; do not be afraid.” The safe place he offers is beside him.

Nob is the city of the priests, and Saul had it put to the sword (1 Samuel 22:19). David doesn't send Abiathar back. He says, “Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.”
